items.title: Fixed window vs sliding window: limit ke edge par double requests kyun nikal jaati hain
items.one_idea: A fixed window rate limiter keeps one counter per time block and resets it at each edge, so a client can send a full limit just before the edge and another full limit just after it (up to twice the limit in a short span); a sliding window fixes this, either exactly by logging every request timestamp (memory grows with traffic) or approximately by weighting the previous window's count (two numbers per client).

items.hook_formula: direct_question: an everyday-looking limit (100 per minute) set against a number that breaks it (200 in 2 seconds), answered by the very next line with the window edge
items.visual_idea: A horizontal timeline cut into equal blocks by tall edge lines, each block with a counter chip; a stack of 10 request squares piles up just left of an edge and 10 more just right of it while a bracket across the edge shows the short span, then a window frame slides along the same timeline, the old squares dropping out of its left side and the count recomputed live.
items.everyday_anchor: A cinema or gym that lets in 100 people per hour counted from the top of the hour: 100 walk in at 9:59 and 100 more at 10:01, so 200 arrive in two minutes although the hourly rule was never broken.
items.example: EXAMPLE: limit 10 requests per 10 seconds (Redis tutorial's own example): 10 requests at second 9 and 10 more at second 11 is 20 in 2 seconds. Sliding window counter EXAMPLE (Cloudflare's numbers): 42 requests in the previous minute, 18 in the current one, 15 seconds into it: 42 x 0.75 + 18 = 49.5.
facts_to_verify: Fixed window: time is split into fixed blocks, one counter per block, the new block starts a fresh count; boundary burst: 10 at second 9 plus 10 at second 11 is 20 in 2 seconds under a '10 per 10 seconds' limit, up to 2x at boundaries (Redis tutorial, fetched by the strategist this session; re-fetch)

Sliding window log: stores each request's timestamp, removes entries older than the window, counts the rest; no boundary bursts; memory grows linearly per client, e.g. a 10,000-per-hour limit holds up to 10,000 entries (Redis tutorial); Cloudflare calls it more accurate but with 'huge processing and memory requirements'

Sliding window counter: previous count x (1 - elapsed fraction) + current count; Cloudflare example 42, 18, 15 s into the minute gives 49.5; it assumes a constant rate in the previous window so it is an approximation; Cloudflare measured 0.003% of 400 million requests wrongly allowed or limited and 'only two numbers per counter' (Cloudflare post)
Redis tutorial's own advice: no single best algorithm; sliding window counter is a good balance for most APIs. Say it as that tutorial's advice, not as an industry fact
Cloudflare's post does not use the words 'boundary problem'; it says the naive fixed window lets regular traffic spikes through. Use the boundary burst wording only with the Redis page
Wikipedia Rate limiting only lists the algorithm names (no explanations): do not cite it for any mechanism
Optional: run a 15-line Python simulation of both counters on the EXAMPLE numbers and show its real output (20 allowed in 2 seconds vs 10)
